Suppose such a regular \(n\)-gon has integer-coordinate vertices. Then its side vectors are integer vectors, so if \(s\) is the side length, then
\[
s^2 \in \mathbb Z_{>0}.
\]
By the shoelace formula, the area \(A\) of the polygon is rational. But the area of a regular \(n\)-gon is also
\[
A=\frac{n}{4}s^2\cot\frac{\pi}{n}.
\]
Thus \(\cot(\pi/n)\) must be rational.

If \(\cot(\pi/n)\in\mathbb Q\), then
\[
\cos\frac{2\pi}{n}=\frac{\cot^2(\pi/n)-1}{\cot^2(\pi/n)+1}\in\mathbb Q.
\]
Let \(\zeta=e^{2\pi i/n}\). Then \(2\cos(2\pi/n)=\zeta+\zeta^{-1}\) is an algebraic integer. A rational algebraic integer is an integer, so
\[
2\cos\frac{2\pi}{n}\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}.
\]
For \(n\ge 3\), this gives only \(n=3,4,6\). Checking these:
\[
\cot\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac1{\sqrt3},\qquad \cot\frac{\pi}{6}=\sqrt3
\]
are irrational, while
\[
\cot\frac{\pi}{4}=1
\]
is rational. Hence only \(n=4\) is possible, and a square with integer vertices clearly exists.

\[
\boxed{4}
\]
